name: Tara Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Tara Patel, 58, and I help replace window seals and damaged trim in an occupied apartment block. I left school early and came from cleaning work, so the senior fitter still checks my cuts and lets me practise on offcuts. I like finding the real source of a draught, though the stairs leave my ankles sore.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because it could thin our visits before robots take the fitting around 2031. Paid trials in real flats, funded supervised training and clear local vacancies would help me keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid to move a tenant’s furniture and open the wall when a repair takes longer than the screen expects. Hidden damp does not read the schedule.

headlineQuote: Hidden damp does not read the schedule.
portrait: Tara is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker learning window and trim repairs in occupied flats.
She uses **AI every day** for checklists and tools, then tests their claims against real damage and experienced fitters.
Her **four-month reserve** and Om’s steady laundry wage soften short gaps but cannot replace long-term site work.
She pursues **paid applications and training** while protecting current shifts and acknowledging that robots could reach physical repairs.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could reduce visits through AI planning before robots threaten her fitting work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid real-flat trials**, supervised funded training and clear local vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that my AI checklist helps me remember which window seals to inspect, even if the technology never becomes magical. The draught still has to be found with a hand and a strip of paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be pleased to keep learning without the job changing overnight. My partner Om and I have about four months of expenses saved, and his laundry job is steady, but the apartment repair contract ends next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid shifts sealing windows and use the checklist each morning, then mark what I actually found on paper. In the first year I would ask the supervisor for another local repair site before this block is finished and keep the savings for a contract gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel mostly calm about AI and restless about the contract clock. A clever checklist cannot sign my next time sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the checklist help last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It reminded me to check a seal above a kitchen window, where rain had slipped behind the trim. I use the tool every day, but I still show the damp patch to the experienced fitter before pulling anything off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you still learning on this crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school early and spent years doing cleaning work, so cutting replacement trim neatly is new to me. The senior fitter lets me practise on offcuts before I touch an occupied flat.

say: I would say **AI checklists** help me remember inspections but cannot find every draught.
I would show the crew the **damp patch** before removing trim.
think: I welcome **steady learning** while the technology changes slowly.
Our **four-month cushion** may have to cover a gap after the apartment contract.
do: Keep taking **paid window shifts** and marking actual findings on paper.
Ask for another **local repair site** before this block finishes.
feel: **Mostly calm** about AI, restless about the contract end.
S0.quote: A clever checklist cannot sign my next time sheet.
fieldNote: Tara uses AI **daily** for inspection memory while checking physical damp with an experienced fitter.
Her **moderate reserve** and Om’s steady laundry wage protect short gaps, but the repair contract ends next spring.

steps.text: Keep taking paid apartment window-sealing shifts
Ask the supervisor about another local repair site before spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster buying could stop us waiting for the right seals, but the crew should be paid for documenting what is wrong in each flat. I would ask the supervisor to show us the new work order screen before he times us by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could answer tenants and schedule visits, leaving fewer office jobs and more timed tasks for us. I am slower than the senior fitter, and a hidden damp patch can make my repair look late even when it is careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the AI work order screen on two occupied flats this month and note where the suggested repair misses damage. In the first year I would keep taking paid sealing shifts and ask the supervisor to count the inspection and tenant conversation as work time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be interested in a better record and worried about a clock that starts before I reach the window. I can move fast on a clean seal, but I will not cover damp to please a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the new record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enter the room, the photo of the stain, the seal size and the minutes spent protecting the tenant’s furniture. If the screen cannot hold those details, I would keep my paper notes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise the timing issue with anyone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two coworkers who handle occupied flats to compare our task times, then show the supervisor together. I want a fair number based on the real repair, not a fight for its own sake.

say: I would say **faster buying** helps only if inspection time is paid.
I would ask to **see the screen** before it sets our task times.
think: I fear **hidden damp** will make careful repairs look late.
I expect **tenant scheduling** to change office jobs before our physical work.
do: Test the **AI work order** on two occupied flats.
Keep taking **paid sealing shifts** during the first year.
Compare **task times** with coworkers before asking for fair targets.
feel: **Interested** in records, worried about careless time limits.
S1.quote: I can move fast on a clean seal, but I will not cover damp to please a screen.
fieldNote: Tara tests the **AI work order** against hidden damage and tenant needs rather than accepting a suggested time.
She will seek **shared evidence** from coworkers before asking the supervisor to change targets.

steps.text: Test the AI work order screen on two occupied flats
Keep taking paid apartment sealing shifts
Compare repair times with coworkers and jointly request fair targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the 2028 intelligence may handle every tenant call and repair plan, while people still fit seals until robots arrive around 2031. I would insist on seeing any machine work inside a lived-in flat before it replaces a worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 in 2028, the office could shrink and the contractor might send us to fewer, tightly planned visits. At 63 in 2031, capable robots could do the sealing and trim too; four months of savings and Om’s wage would not cover our lives indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid window shifts and make a dated portfolio of completed repairs now. In 2029 I would apply for a paid facilities role at the public library while staying on site; if robots take the repairs in 2031, I would ask the employment service about funded training and income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel alarmed, then start listing every bill because that is how I think when frightened. A machine that can fit a seal can also take the little craft I have fought to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the library role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library has a posted vacancy close to our bus line, and I could keep earning while human maintenance is still needed. I would not call it a refuge after capable robots can do hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Om?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Om that the laundry wage is not our retirement plan and that I am applying before the apartment contract ends. We would check rent, food and transport together before spending savings on any course.

say: I would say **thinking AI** reaches tenant calls before robots fit seals.
I would ask for a **lived-in-flat trial** before anyone loses a shift.
think: At **60**, tighter plans could reduce our paid repair visits.
At **63**, capable robots could take my trim work beyond what our buffer covers.
do: Keep **paid window shifts** and build a dated repair portfolio.
Apply for **library facilities** work in 2029 while employed.
Ask the **employment service** about support if robots take repairs.
feel: **Alarmed**, then focused on listing the household bills.
S2.quote: A machine that can fit a seal can also take the little craft I have fought to learn.
fieldNote: Tara sees **2028 office changes** as a possible visit reduction before robots directly take physical repairs around 2031.
The **library application** seeks near-term wages; she knows facilities work may also be automated later.

steps.text: Keep taking paid apartment window shifts through 2029
Apply for the posted public library facilities role in 2029
Ask the employment service about support if robots take repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years lets us document the real trouble spots and try new equipment with a human checking it. I would ask the contractor to pay for tool practice, because a training day without wages is not free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, AI could plan and assess every window while I still climb the steps and replace trim. At 66 in 2034, robots could do the climbing and fitting too, and I do not know how much retirement income Om and I will have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the senior fitter now to show me the AI-assisted moisture camera on the worst flat and keep my paid repair shifts. In 2032 I would apply for a college building-care post and enroll in a funded damp-repair course if it includes supervised work and does not cancel my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel able to prepare, although the end date would still worry me. Learning a camera is useful now; it is not a guarantee that somebody pays me at 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from the camera?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its reading with the stain behind the trim and ask why the numbers differ. I like tools that help me see, not tools that make the decision before the wall is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you refuse the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refuse if the fee came from our four-month cushion or if classes took the paid days we need for rent. A certificate is only worth trying when I can practise with a real fitter.

say: I would ask for **paid tool practice** with a human checking results.
I would say **five years** allows real damage records before equipment changes.
think: At **63**, AI may assess windows while I still do the fitting.
At **66**, robots could take fitting before our retirement income is known.
do: Learn the **AI moisture camera** with the senior fitter.
Keep taking **paid shifts** and apply for college building care in 2032.
Enroll in **funded damp training** if supervised and compatible with shifts.
feel: **Able to prepare**, though future wages remain uncertain.
S3.quote: Learning a camera is useful now; it is not a guarantee that somebody pays me at 66.
fieldNote: Tara wants to test **camera readings** against opened walls and a senior fitter’s judgment.
She makes **damp-repair training conditional** on funding, supervision and continued paid site work.

steps.text: Learn the AI moisture camera with the senior fitter
Keep taking paid repair shifts in 2032
Apply for a college building-care post in 2032
Enroll in funded supervised damp-repair training if shifts remain paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years could let us earn, save and decide carefully, if the contractor keeps older learners on the jobs. I would ask for a simple yearly count of paid repair days, not just pictures of new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I might work fewer window jobs because climbing steps all day strains my ankles. At 71 in 2039, robots could take the physical repairs anyway, and savings would have to cover any gap between our real income and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking ground-floor paid repairs and set aside part of each full-pay month for a household reserve. In 2037 I would review our rent and Om’s laundry wage, apply for a paid materials-counter opening if one appears, and decide about fewer shifts only after seeing several months of figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more patient and still alert. Ten years makes a plan possible, but the plan has to be paid for one ordinary month at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the counter job be safe from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take the ordering and robots could move stock later, so I would apply for paid years rather than promise myself safety. The counter has stools and less climbing, which might help my ankles while work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have homes of their own, and I would not use their pay in our budget. We would ask for help if we truly could not cover housing, but first Om and I would count what we have.

say: I would ask for **yearly paid-day counts** for older repair workers.
I would say **ten years** gives us time to earn and choose carefully.
think: At **68**, sore ankles may limit steps before thinking AI arrives.
At **71**, robots could take repairs while our savings remain finite.
do: Keep taking **ground-floor repairs** and add to the reserve after full-pay months.
Review **rent and wages** with Om in 2037.
Apply for a **paid materials counter** post if one appears.
feel: **Patient**, while alert to the need for continuing wages.
S4.quote: Ten years makes a plan possible, but the plan has to be paid for one ordinary month at a time.
fieldNote: Tara’s long warning includes **ankle strain** as a limit on future site work before robots arrive.
The **counter application** offers less climbing, yet she acknowledges exposure to AI ordering and later stock-moving robots.

steps.text: Keep taking paid ground-floor repair shifts in 2037
Set aside part of full-pay months for the household reserve
Apply for a paid materials-counter post if one appears
